## Chapter 1

## Chapter 2

VIS NOVA (1903-1904)

Paris after midsummer was a place where history might best be observed, had Western society not shut its eyes. Manchuria knew every step into war; Japan had completed every preparation; from Yokohama to Irkutsk the East was under war conditions. But Europe knew nothing. The banks would allow no disturbance; the press said not a word; even the embassies were silent. For once, the conspiracy of silence became crime. Adams felt as ignorant as the best-informed statesman, and could not understand how the comedy could be so well acted. He found himself face to face with his new problem—the workings of Russian inertia—and could conceive no way of forming an opinion how much was real and how much was comedy.

On January 6, 1904, he reached Washington, where the contrast astonished him. He had never before seen his country think as a world-power. He took his brother Brooks's place at the Diplomatic Reception and supped at the President's table. Roosevelt talked and the guests listened; with the usual abuse of the *quos ego* common to vigorous statesmen, he said all that he thought about Russians and Japanese, Boers and British, in full hearing of twenty people, and concluded: "I could do it myself; I could stop it to-morrow!" To one who had just escaped the European conspiracy of silence, it was like drawing a free breath after stifling. The truth was commonplace if one liked, but it was not a truth of inertia.

Nor could the force of Japan be mistaken for inertia. Each day counted as a measure of relative energy on the historical scale, and the war made a Grammar of new Science quite as instructive as Pearson's. For Adams it had no personal value except that it gave Hay his last great triumph. He had carried on his long contest with Cassini so skillfully that no one knew enough to understand the diplomatic perfection of his work. Japan and England saved his "open door" and fought his battle.

The President made Hay go to St. Louis to address the Exposition, and Mrs. Hay bade Adams go with them. He professed the religion of World's Fairs, without which he held education to be a blind impossibility. Through Ohio and Indiana, agriculture had made way for steam; tall chimneys reeked smoke on every horizon. The American of the prime seemed extinct with the Shawnee and the buffalo. The new American showed his parentage proudly; he was the child of steam and the brother of the dynamo, squeezed and welded into approach to shape, a product of mechanical power. The St. Louis Exposition was its first creation in the twentieth century. Here was a third-rate town of half-a-million people without history, education, unity, or art, throwing away forty million dollars on a pageant as ephemeral as a stage flat. By night Arabia's crimson sands had never returned a glow half so astonishing—long lines of white palaces, exquisitely lighted by thousands of electric candles. One enjoyed it with iniquitous rapture, not because of exhibits but rather because of their want.

He left St. Louis on May 22, and on Sunday, June 5, found himself again at Coutances, where the people of Normandy had built, towards the year 1250, an Exposition expressive of force as well as grace in the Virgin. The streets were filled with altars to her, the cathedral densely thronged at mass. The Virgin did not shut her costly Exposition on Sunday or any other day. Her power had been plainly One, embracing all human activity, while the power of the Senate seemed more or less ashamed of man and his work.

That her force was still actual proved itself at once by forcing Adams to buy an automobile—the supreme demonstration, since it was the form of force he most abominated. He had set aside the summer for study of the Virgin as motive power, and the automobile alone could unite her monuments in any reasonable sequence. For him, the Virgin was an adorable mistress, who led the automobile and its owner where she would, from Chartres to Rouen, thence to Amiens and Laon. He never doubted her force, since he felt it to the last fibre of his being. If the automobile had one *vitesse* more useful than another, it was that of a century a minute. The centuries dropped like autumn leaves in one's road.

One late afternoon, wandering through Troyes in close conversation with Thibaut of Champagne, he noticed men looking at a bit of paper stuck in a window. M. de Plehve had been assassinated at St. Petersburg. The mad mixture of Russia and the Crusades drove him for refuge into the Church of St. Pantaleon. Martyrs, murderers, Cæsars, saints and assassins—half in glass and half in telegram—gave him vertigo. Was assassination forever to be the last word of Progress? The Virgin herself never looked so winning—so One—as in this scandalous failure of her Grace. To what purpose had she existed, if, after nineteen hundred years, the world was bloodier than when she was born? The stupendous failure of Christianity tortured history.

As long as he could whisper, he would go on as he had begun, bluntly refusing to meet his creator with the admission that the creation had taught him nothing. One sought no absolute truth; only a spool on which to wind the thread of history without breaking it. Among indefinite possible orbits, one sought the orbit which would best satisfy the observed movement of the runaway star Groombridge, 1838, commonly called Henry Adams. When the fogs and frosts shut him up again in his garret, he sat down as a boy at school to shape a Dynamic Theory of History: man as a feeble atom captured by the attractive forces of nature, his progress measurable as the assimilation of new energies—from fetish and Cross to compass and gunpowder—each accelerating his orbit toward an unknown perihelion.
